subject: biology-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Gas exchange
bigPicture: As organisms get bigger, their surface area-to-volume ratio falls, so they need specialised exchange surfaces. Lungs and leaves both maximise surface area and keep concentration gradients steep; HL adds how haemoglobin loads and unloads oxygen.

keyIdeas.cue: Why is gas exchange harder for large organisms?
keyIdeas.answer: Surface area-to-volume ratio falls as size increases, and the distance from the centre to the surface grows, so diffusion across the body surface alone becomes too slow.

keyIdeas.cue: What properties do gas-exchange surfaces share?
keyIdeas.answer: Permeable to gases, thin (short diffusion distance), moist (gases dissolve before diffusing) and a large surface area.

keyIdeas.cue: How do animals keep concentration gradients steep?
keyIdeas.answer: A dense network of blood vessels, continuous blood flow carrying gases away/towards the surface, and ventilation: air in lungs, water over gills.

Branched bronchioles lead to millions of alveoli (huge surface area); dense capillary beds; thin walls (type I pneumocytes); surfactant from type II pneumocytes reduces surface tension so alveoli don't collapse and stick.

Inhale: diaphragm contracts and flattens, external intercostals lift ribs up and out, volume rises, pressure falls, air flows in. Exhale (forced): internal intercostals pull ribs down and abdominal muscles push the diaphragm up; at rest, exhalation is mostly passive recoil.

keyIdeas.cue: Name the lung volumes you can measure.
keyIdeas.answer: Tidal volume (normal breath), vital capacity (maximum breath out after maximum breath in), inspiratory reserve (extra in beyond tidal) and expiratory reserve (extra out beyond tidal). Measured with a spirometer or bell jar.

keyIdeas.cue: How is a leaf adapted for gas exchange?
keyIdeas.answer: Waxy cuticle and epidermis limit water loss; stomata with guard cells control gas entry; air spaces in the spongy mesophyll give a large moist internal surface; veins bring water and remove sugars.

keyIdeas.cue: What does a plan diagram of a dicot leaf show?
keyIdeas.answer: Tissue layers only, no individual cells: upper epidermis (with cuticle), palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll with air spaces, lower epidermis with stomata, and vascular bundles (xylem above phloem).

keyIdeas.cue: Why is transpiration a consequence of gas exchange, and what affects its rate?
keyIdeas.answer: Open stomata let CO₂ in, so water vapour inevitably escapes from moist mesophyll surfaces. Rate rises with higher temperature, light (stomata open), wind, and lower humidity.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you measure stomatal density?
keyIdeas.answer: Count stomata in a field of view of a micrograph or nail-varnish leaf cast, divide by field area (density = number ÷ area, e.g. per mm²). Repeat counts in several fields because biological material varies.

keyIdeas.cue: How are foetal and adult haemoglobin adapted?
keyIdeas.answer: Cooperative binding: each O₂ that binds changes the shape of haemoglobin, making it easier for the next to bind. CO₂ binds allosterically (away from the haem) and lowers affinity. Foetal haemoglobin has a higher O₂ affinity than adult, so it takes O₂ from the mother's blood in the placenta.

Higher CO₂ (and the acidity it causes) lowers haemoglobin's affinity for O₂, shifting the curve right. In actively respiring tissues, where CO₂ is high, more O₂ is released exactly where it is needed.

keyIdeas.cue: Why is the oxygen dissociation curve S-shaped?
keyIdeas.answer: At low pO₂ the first O₂ binds with difficulty (flat start); once bound, cooperative binding makes further binding easier (steep middle); then haemoglobin approaches saturation (plateau). The curve is in the data booklet.

Secreted by type II pneumocytes; reduces surface tension in alveoli.
Volume of air in and out in a normal breath.

workedExamples.title: Stomatal density
workedExamples.prompt: A leaf cast shows 42 stomata in a circular field of view of radius 0.20 mm. Calculate stomatal density.
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 333 mm⁻². Repeat in other fields and average.

workedExamples.title: Lung volumes from a spirometer trace
workedExamples.prompt: Tidal breaths go between 2.4 and 2.9 L; the deepest breath in reaches 5.4 L; the deepest breath out reaches 1.2 L. Find tidal volume, IRV, ERV and vital capacity.
workedExamples.answer: TV 0.5 L, IRV 2.5 L, ERV 1.2 L, VC 4.2 L.

misconceptions.wrong: Air is sucked in by the lungs.
misconceptions.right: Muscles increase thorax volume, lowering pressure; air is pushed in by higher atmospheric pressure.
It reduces surface tension so alveoli don't collapse.
They respire all the time; in daylight photosynthesis just exceeds it.

misconceptions.wrong: Transpiration is the purpose of stomata.
misconceptions.right: It is an unavoidable side effect of opening stomata for CO₂.

misconceptions.wrong: The Bohr shift increases oxygen loading in the lungs.
misconceptions.right: It increases unloading in respiring tissues, where CO₂ is high.
